body_markdown:
This is not your father’s Jensen. If that’s not apparent from the massive carbon rear wing, skirts, diffuser, and front splitter, it will be the moment that the engine fires.


The 6.8-liter supercharged V-8 explodes into life with a guttural sound that hits you in the chest and leaves your ears ringing.


After two years in development—and more than seven years since the idea was conceived—the new Interceptor GTX from Jensen International is ready.


There are nods to the past, most obviously with the name, of course, but this is the future. Jensen International is slowly winding down its current business, having completed 50 examples of its Interceptor R and S restomods, and is now focused on bringing the GTX to market.


The first stage is a track car, which is a massive departure for a brand best-known for its mile-munching GTs, but it’s a pragmatic approach to test the market.


Jensen International


Jensen International


Jensen International


“A track day car is kind of odd for Jensen to have, but it’s really just a starting point,” says backer[Jeff Qvale](https://www.hagerty.com/media/people/the-qvale-familys-80-year-love-affair-with-cars/) , whose father once owned the Jensen factory.


“My dad never kept anything. He said, ‘I’m not in a warehouse business, I’m in the selling business.’ He had very little that he kept, so we didn’t have an Interceptor. I thought maybe I should get one—these guys are really making a nice restomod. I did, and it really is great, especially with new suspension and the really nice new GM motor.


“I kept in touch with them, and then when I moved over to the U.K. with my wife and kids, I got more and more involved with them, and found out that they tried to do a new Interceptor a few years ago, and it didn’t exactly pan out.


“The designer at Avant, they’d done some work on it, and they redid it and updated it. So I said, okay, look, we’re not going to do a normal production thing, unless somebody wants to get involved and write a big check and go forward with it. We’re going to do it small and one-off. I figured you’ve got to do a car; you can’t sell it off the computer—you’ve really got to do a car that you can get the feel of. I’ll commit to one car, and we’ll see if it works.”


“We know it’s cheaper and quicker to build a track car, with fixed windows and a basic interior,” adds Jensen International boss David Duerden. “So, we said, let’s try that. Then it became apparent that there was a niche of non-road legal track cars, and we could address that as well. It gives you a double attempt at it. This isn’t by any means the end of the line. It’s a little adjunct off the beginning, the first prototype, and the idea is to go on from there into a road car.”


Jensen International


Jensen International


Jensen International


Actually, there are two road cars in the plan; a four-seater GT that more closely echoes the original Interceptor concept, and a street-legal version of the GTX.


For now, though, there is the GTX. “We call it an enhanced prototype because it is far more than a prototype,” explains Duerden. “You can see it’s a finished car. It doesn’t really look like a prototype in any real way, other than it’s built as a race car. The body shape and paneling are all done. We’ve got tooling for that. We would develop the chassis a little bit further (for the road), but we’re really not that far off.”


The bodywork, hand-formed in aluminum, certainly does look like a finished product. The blue paint (actually an Alpine color, named after Fernando Alonso) gleams, and the shut lines are tight. At first glance, you might mistake the profile for an Aston Martin, but look closer at the rear quarter and you’ll find a tribute to the original Interceptor in the floating roof and placement of the badging. The face, meanwhile, feels almost American in design, hinting at the muscle behind it, while the rear is dominated by aggressive aero and 3D-printed titanium exhaust tips.


Jensen International


Jensen International


Jensen International


Polycarbonate is used instead of glass throughout, and aerospace-grade fixings are deliberately visible, with Duerden noting that each bolt costs £5. Imagine the GTX with flush glass, remove the downforce-developing carbon parts, raise the ride height, and it’s easy to see it as a road car.


Jensen International


Jensen International


The interior will require a bit more imagination, as currently it’s mostly exposed carbon and plastic, plus MoTec race car controls and instrumentation. There’s a full FIA-spec roll cage, plumbed-in fire extinguisher, and fixed-back Tillett race seats with six-point harnesses. Ear plugs would be strongly advised.


Noise apart, the front-mid mounted V-8 has certainly got the goods. It’s a GM LT to begin with, but after Houston, Texas-based Late Model Engines gets hold of it, only around 20% of the original parts are maintained. It’s bored out to 6.8 liters, fitted with all-new internals along with CNC-machined heads and titanium valves. Then a 2.65-liter Roots-type supercharger is added, together with the MoTec engine management system and a new exhaust. It’s currently making around 950 horsepower, but it can be dialed up to almost 1200.


Jensen International


A carbon fiber prop shaft sends power to the rear transaxle transmission by Samsonas Motorsport. Car zero is a six-speed sequential with straight-cut gears operated by a lever or paddles, but there’s no reason an H-pattern ‘box can’t be fitted—or, indeed, an automatic. Jensen uses a Wavetrac differential and the MoTec system provides multi-stage traction control.


The AP Racing braking system also has programmable ABS. Steel discs are deployed with Duerden reasoning that “even in GT racing they don’t use carbon discs.”


Jensen International


The GTX is built on a platform of bonded, extruded aluminum, with manually adjustable Nitron dampers for the double wishbone suspension. 20-inch custom aluminum wheels from Vossen are shod with Michelin Pilot Sport tires.


Now that it’s been officially unveiled, Jensen International will gauge the reaction, while continuing to hone the GTX on track.


To date, around £1.3M has been invested in the program, and Qvale is realistic about his expectations: “I’m not aiming at making money (right away), because I know that’s almost impossible, but I’m aiming at making a good car and finding out whether 10, 20, 50 people want it. Then we can talk about maybe making money.”


Qvale says of the GTX: “It’s going to be expensive, but it won’t be a million quid,” with Duerden suggesting a price of around £850,000.


“We want to see what both consumer and investor sentiment is,” concludes Duerden. “What does the world think of it? We know what we think it should be, and where we’d like to go with it, but we’re by no means slaves to that. We’ve got to have a degree of humility with this, and go, let’s see what everyone wants to do here. But in the meantime, it’s a good-looking thing, isn’t it?”


Judge for yourselves.


Jensen International
